title: Called up to the Torah
hook: people are called up to say a blessing before and after each section

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rashi's question at Sinai: read it, find one question, see what Rashi asks, find one thing for your life. Your line was one verse a week.

It's Shabbat morning. The scroll is open on the reading table, and the room goes quiet. Someone at the table calls out a Hebrew name, the person's own and their parents'. A person in the congregation stands up, a little nervous, and walks to the front. Maybe it's their first time since their bar or bat mitzvah. Maybe their grandmother is watching. Maybe they've just had a baby, or are about to get married, or it's the anniversary of a parent's death. They step up to the scroll. They don't have to read a word of it. They just have to bless.
screen: `A HEBREW NAME IS CALLED.` → `SOMEONE WALKS TO THE FRONT.` → `THEY DON'T READ. THEY BLESS.`

segments.voice: The word is aliyah, going up. The reading table often stands on a raised platform, the bimah, so you literally go up to it. But the word means more than stairs: being called to the Torah is an honor, a going up in spirit. On Shabbat morning the portion is divided into seven sections, and seven people are called, one for each, with an extra one at the end. On Mondays and Thursdays, three. Traditionally the first goes to a kohen, a descendant of the priests, the second to a levi, and the rest to anyone. Here's what happens. The person looks at the place in the scroll and says the blessing before. It begins Barchu, bless the Lord who is blessed, and it thanks God for choosing Israel and giving the Torah. The reader chants the section while the person stands beside them, following along. Then the blessing after: thanking God, who gave us a Torah of truth and planted eternal life in our midst. And they step aside for the next. In Orthodox synagogues, men are called up. In Reform, Reconstructionist and egalitarian Conservative synagogues, women are called up too. The same word has another life: when a Jew moves to the land of Israel, that's also called making aliyah, going up. So this week's four days fit together: a handwritten scroll, heard aloud. Fifty-four portions. A way to read one. And now, a way to stand beside it, and go up.
screen: `ALIYAH: GOING UP.` · `SEVEN ON SHABBAT, THREE ON WEEKDAYS.` · `A BLESSING BEFORE AND AFTER.` · `A TORAH OF TRUTH, ETERNAL LIFE.` · then, large: `GO UP.`

segments.voice: Picture a book or a page you'll read today, and imagine standing up and walking toward it, as if your name had been called. If you pray, you can say the old words, blessed are you, Lord our God, who gave us a Torah of truth. If you don't, just stand, or sit up straight, and take one breath of respect before the first word.
Aliyah. Going up: being called to the Torah to say the blessings before and after a section of the reading.
Your line: go up. Tomorrow, the first portion opens. One hundred sixty days now.

options: No. You say the blessings before and after; the reader usually chants it.

chat.meaning: An aliyah means going up to the Torah to say the blessings before and after a section. The reader usually chants it.

notes: Numbers of aliyot: seven on Shabbat morning plus maftir; three on Mondays, Thursdays and Shabbat afternoon; festivals differ. The script says 'an extra one at the end' for maftir; confirm.
The blessings are described and partly translated ('Barchu...'; 'who gave us a Torah of truth and planted eternal life in our midst'), not quoted from a published translation. Confirm wording.
Women receiving aliyot: not in Orthodox synagogues (with some partnership-minyan exceptions); standard in most Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist synagogues. Confirm phrasing.
The practice offers a rendering of the after-blessing as a line to say 'if you pray'; confirm this is acceptable as a real blessing rather than a new prayer.
